native_mcp_support.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 against Microsoft Learn (page updated 2026-08-11). MCP is now a first-class extensibility path across FOUR Microsoft Copilot surfaces: (1) Microsoft 365 Copilot declarative agents via MCP-server plugins (`RemoteMCPServer` runtime in plugin manifest 2.4), incl. MCP apps/UI widgets and runtime dynamic tool discovery; (2) Microsoft 365 Copilot federated connectors, which are MCP-based read-only data connectors surfaced in Copilot Chat, Copilot in Excel and the Researcher agent; (3) Microsoft Copilot Studio, where MCP is GA and servers are attached as Power Platform custom connectors; (4) GitHub Copilot (VS Code, JetBrains, Xcode, Eclipse, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot CLI, Copilot app, cloud agent). Copilot Cowork (GA 2026-06-16) adds MCP `remoteMcpServer` connectors in its app packages. A fifth path, the Microsoft Work IQ API, exposes Microsoft 365 data to external agents over both Agent-to-Agent and MCP. Consumer Copilot (copilot.microsoft.com) still exposes no developer MCP surface.

skills_concept.value: Declarative agents + MCP/API plugins (M365 Copilot); Skills + connectors in app packages (Copilot Cowork); agents + tools (Copilot Studio); agent mode + MCP servers (GitHub Copilot); no developer skills surface (consumer Copilot)
skills_concept.notes: Changed 2026-08-19: Microsoft now ships an explicit, Anthropic-style 'Skill' primitive in Copilot Cowork — prompt-based `SKILL.md` workflow packages with a documented context budget (body target under 5,000 tokens; up to 20 skills and 10 MCP connectors per app package; up to 50 custom skills and plugins per user). That sits alongside the older 'declarative agent' analog in Microsoft 365 Copilot (instructions + plugins + knowledge, actions array capped at 10), Copilot Studio agents (tools + knowledge sources), and GitHub Copilot agent mode (MCP servers as the tool/skill provider). These are the vendor's 'skills' analogs for this dataset.

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 (architecture page updated 2026-07-13). Microsoft still publishes no raw per-request context-window token number for Microsoft 365 Copilot, and the underlying model is now user-selectable (OpenAI GPT-5.x or Anthropic Claude), so a single number would be wrong anyway. What IS documented and binding for MCP work is the plugin scope: a 4,096-token limit that 'includes all context and response data', with guidance to 'Optimize for approximately 66% of the technical limit' (~2,730 tokens).

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Not published by Microsoft for Microsoft 365 Copilot; inherited from the selected underlying model (OpenAI GPT-5.x or Anthropic Claude).

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Not published. The documented output-side constraints are product-layer item counts: plugin response limit 25 items, grounding record limit 50 items, all inside the 4,096-token plugin budget.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Standard ~4 chars/token rule of thumb for English text on o200k_base-family encodings; empirical, not a Microsoft-published figure.

function_calling.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 (page updated 2026-08-05). Declarative agents call tools through plugins, which are either MCP servers or OpenAPI-described REST APIs.

native_mcp.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 (page updated 2026-08-11). A declarative agent plugin can point at a remote MCP server (`RemoteMCPServer` runtime, plugin manifest 2.4); the agent resolves the server's tools at runtime. MCP apps (tools returning UI widgets) render inline. Auth: none, API key, OAuth (static or dynamic client registration), or Microsoft Entra SSO. Separately, MCP-enabled agents reached Word/Excel/PowerPoint/Outlook on 2026-07-15 per the release notes.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: CHANGED from null to false. The architecture page (updated 2026-07-13) still states: 'Because Microsoft grounding and calls to external tools happen sequentially, you can't use chained operations with grounding data or looped operation plans.' Sequential-only processing is documented, so parallel tool calling is not available on this surface.

max_tools_hard.notes: No numeric per-request cap on the NUMBER of tools/functions is published for Microsoft 365 Copilot. The plugins page (re-opened 2026-08-19, updated 2026-08-05) explicitly declines to bound functions or MCP tools per plugin ('A plugin can include an unlimited number of functions or MCP tools'). The limits that DO bind, all AGGREGATE across the declarative agent rather than per MCP server: the manifest's 10-action/plugin-object ceiling per declarative agent (recorded under max_connected_servers, and derived there -- Microsoft never states it in MCP-server units), the 4,096-token plugin I/O budget that every injected tool definition competes for (a token budget, not a byte payload cap -- see max_request_size.notes, whose value is null for that reason), the documented quality cliff above 10 functions/tools, and the 5-plugin always-injected threshold beyond which semantic matching decides what is injected.

max_tools_practical.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19; wording now reads 'Due to token window limits, the quality of the responses might degrade if more than 10 functions or tools are included' (previous wording said 'functions'; MCP tools are now named explicitly). Scope: per plugin / per MCP server, not aggregate. Vendor-published but behavioural rather than enforced, hence recorded as the practical limit.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No dedicated tool-name length cap is published. Plugin manifest 2.4 (updated 2026-07-01) constrains function `name` by pattern only — must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$` (and `namespace` must match `^[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) — and applies the manifest-wide default of 4,000 characters to unqualified string properties. MCP tool names come from the server and are not separately bounded in Microsoft's docs.

max_tool_description_len.notes: CHANGED from null. Plugin manifest schema 2.4 (updated 2026-07-01) states that for `description_for_model`, 'Characters beyond 2048 MAY be ignored' — that is the model-facing tool/plugin description, i.e. exactly the field whose tokens land in the prompt. (Human-facing fields are tighter still: `name_for_human` beyond 20 chars and `description_for_human` beyond 100 chars MAY be ignored.) Confidence medium because the cap is expressed as MAY-be-ignored rather than a hard rejection, and because MCP tool descriptions arriving from the server are governed by the 4,096-token plugin budget rather than this manifest field.

max_request_size.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19: was 4096 with unit "tokens"; now null. Across this dataset max_request_size is the BYTE ceiling on the request payload (Anthropic 32 MB, Gemini 100 MB, OpenAI 512 MB, Copilot Studio 5 MB connector payload), so a token budget stored in the same field made Microsoft 365 Copilot look ~5 orders of magnitude smaller than its peers and corrupted any cross-vendor min()/comparison. One field name, one meaning. Microsoft publishes NO byte/KB/MB request or response ceiling for the Microsoft 365 Copilot plugin/MCP path -- re-checked 2026-08-19 on this architecture page (its technical-limits table is expressed only in items, tokens and seconds), the plugins overview, the API plugin manifest 2.4 schema (character limits only, plus "Implementations are free to impose their own practical limits on manifest length") and the MCP-apps troubleshooting page (which only advises "Ensure responses aren't excessively large" with no number). WHAT THE 4,096 ACTUALLY IS, and where it now lives: a product-layer TOKEN budget for the plugin scope, verbatim "Token limit: 4,096* - Includes all context and response data", with the asterisk defined as "Limits include external overhead such as network latency and Microsoft service processing. Optimize for about 66% of the technical limit" (~2,730 tokens). Every injected tool definition, tool argument and tool result competes inside that one budget, and it is the ceiling that really binds this surface -- it is preserved in prose here, in tool_schema_limits_notes item (6), and in the max_tools_hard / max_total_tools notes, but it is NOT a byte ceiling and is not comparable to one. A 45-second timeout ("Timeout limit: 45 seconds* - Includes network latency and processing time") applies to the same scope.

max_tool_result_size.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19: was 25 with unit "items"; now null. Across this dataset max_tool_result_size is a SIZE ceiling on a single tool RESULT (OpenAI 512 KB, Copilot Cowork 150 MiB per tool call); an item COUNT recorded in the same field is a different quantity and would corrupt any cross-vendor min()/comparison -- 25 would have read as the smallest result cap in the roster. Microsoft documents no byte or token ceiling on an individual plugin/MCP tool result for Microsoft 365 Copilot: the MCP-apps troubleshooting page only advises "Ensure responses aren't excessively large" (re-opened 2026-08-19), and no byte/KB/MB figure appears on the architecture page, the plugins overview or the API plugin manifest 2.4 schema. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED, and what actually binds a chatty tool here, verbatim from this page: "Plugin response limit: 25 items - Constrains external API response sizes" and "Grounding record limit: 50 items - Affects the amount of contextual data available" -- item counts, not sizes -- together with the 4,096-token plugin I/O budget, which truncates rather than rejects: "The token window for inputs to and outputs from a plugin truncates large content" (overview-plugins). Both item counts are also carried in tool_schema_limits_notes items (4) and (5); the token budget is described in max_request_size.notes and item (6).

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Recorded as 1 to represent the documented sequential-only model ('Microsoft grounding and calls to external tools happen sequentially'). Microsoft does not state a parallel-call count, so this encodes the constraint rather than a published integer.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No published cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. The binding documented constraint is the 45-second timeout for the plugin scope (including network latency and processing), reinforced by the sequential-processing model; the architecture page lists 'long-running processes' and 'complex decision trees requiring multiple conditional branches' as poor fits for declarative agents.

max_connected_servers.notes: DERIVED, and NOT a published MCP-server cap. Confidence lowered high -> medium on 2026-08-19 after re-opening the cited page. What the page actually says (re-read 2026-08-19): the `actions` property is 'A list of 1-10 objects that identify plugins that provide actions accessible to the declarative agent', and the Actions object section adds 'The array must contain at least one and no more than 10 objects.' The words MCP / Model Context Protocol do not appear on that page at all, so the unit here is action (plugin) OBJECTS, not MCP servers. The bridge to MCP is a different tier-1 page, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/extensibility/build-mcp-plugins (re-read 2026-08-19): an MCP server is attached to a declarative agent by adding an action ('Add an Action' -> 'Start with an MCP Server'), whose generated `ai-plugin.json` uses the RemoteMCPServer runtime and resolves the server's tools at runtime; that page publishes no numeric limit of its own. So an agent whose every action is an MCP server tops out at 10 MCP servers -- an inference across two tier-1 pages, not a sentence Microsoft has written. Related documented behaviour: at 5 or fewer plugins all are injected into the prompt; above 5, semantic matching selects which are injected per turn (overview-plugins, 2026-08-05).

max_total_tools.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19 from 10 to null. The previous 10 was the declarative-agent manifest's `actions` cap -- a count of plugin OBJECTS -- recorded on this dataset's TOOL-COUNT axis, which rendered Microsoft 365 Copilot as a 10-tool ceiling next to GitHub Copilot's 128 and Grok's 200. That is a unit conflation and a false cross-vendor comparison; the plugin-object ceiling now lives in max_connected_servers. Microsoft publishes NO aggregate cap on the number of individual tools: the plugins overview (tier 1, re-opened 2026-08-19) states verbatim 'A plugin can include an unlimited number of functions or MCP tools. All of a matched plugin's functions or tools are returned, even if only one is matched.' -- i.e. no per-request numeric tool-count cap is documented for this surface. The limits that DO bind, all aggregate across the declarative agent: (1) at most 10 action/plugin objects per agent (schema 1.8, 'A list of 1-10 objects that identify plugins') -- see max_connected_servers; (2) 5 or fewer plugins are always injected into the prompt, above that semantic matching decides which are injected per turn, and a matched plugin brings ALL of its tools with it; (3) the 4,096-token plugin I/O budget, inside which every injected tool definition, argument and result competes (documented in max_request_size.notes; that numeric field is null because it is this dataset's byte-payload ceiling and Microsoft publishes no byte figure for this surface); (4) the documented quality cliff -- 'Due to token window limits, the quality of the responses might degrade if more than 10 functions or tools are included' (max_tools_practical).

tool_definition_shape.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Plugin manifest 2.4 added the `RemoteMCPServer` runtime type, so a plugin is backed either by an MCP server (raw MCP tool schemas fetched from the server) or by an OpenAPI document (OpenAI-function-shaped operations declared in the `functions` array).

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. The 4,096-token plugin limit explicitly 'includes all context and response data', and plugins are injected into the prompt (all of them when there are 5 or fewer). Tool definitions therefore consume the budget before any tool is called.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Confidence raised medium→high and re-sourced. Two documented deferral mechanisms now exist: (1) semantic matching — with more than 5 plugins on an agent, only matched plugins are injected per turn (overview-plugins, 2026-08-05); (2) dynamic tool discovery for MCP plugins (page updated 2026-07-16) — with `"functions": []` and `run_for_functions: ["*"]` on a `RemoteMCPServer` runtime, the agent resolves the server's tool list at runtime per session from the MCP server instead of pinning a static list at publish time. Microsoft publishes no token-saving figure for either.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: PRODUCT-LAYER LIMITS (Microsoft 365 Copilot declarative agents), re-verified 2026-08-19. (1) Actions (plugin OBJECTS; an MCP server is attached as one action, per build-mcp-plugins) per agent: 1-10 — declarative agent schema 1.8, GA, which caps `actions` without ever mentioning MCP; the MCP-server reading is derived. (2) Always-injected plugins: 5 or fewer; above that, semantic matching selects which are injected. (3) Functions / MCP tools per plugin: no numeric cap is published — 'A plugin can include an unlimited number of functions or MCP tools' (overview-plugins, 2026-08-05) — but Microsoft documents that response quality might degrade above 10 functions or tools. (4) Plugin response: 25 items. (5) Grounding records: 50 items. (6) Plugin I/O token budget: 4,096 TOKENS covering context AND response; optimize to ~66% (~2,730 tokens). This is a token budget, not a byte payload ceiling -- Microsoft publishes no byte/KB/MB request or response limit for this surface, so max_request_size (this dataset's byte field) is null. (7) Turn timeout for the plugin scope: 45 seconds including network latency. (8) Sequential tool/grounding processing only. (9) Manifest strings: 4,000-character default; instructions 8,000; name 100; description 1,000; disclaimer.text 500. (10) Model-facing plugin/function description (`description_for_model`): characters beyond 2,048 MAY be ignored; `name_for_human` beyond 20 and `description_for_human` beyond 100 MAY be ignored (plugin manifest 2.4). (11) Function names must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$`; namespaces `^[A-Za-z0-9]+$`. (12) Conversation starters: 12. (13) Capability caps in 1.8: WebSearch sites 4; TeamsMessages urls 5; Meetings items_by_id 5; Email group_mailboxes 25; EmbeddedKnowledge 10 files at 1 MB each; editorial_answers 300. (14) MCP plugin auth: none, API key, OAuth (static or dynamic registration), Microsoft Entra SSO.
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: NEW SINCE 2026-06-21. (a) Declarative agent manifest 1.8 shipped July 2026, adding EmailActions and MeetingActions write capabilities, a `file` property on worker agents, and `embedded_resource_snapshot_id` on embedded knowledge; no change to the 10-action cap. (b) MCP-enabled agents became available inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Catalyst (2026-07-15 release notes). (c) Federated Copilot connectors — MCP-based, read-only, user-identity, non-indexing data connectors surfaced in Copilot Chat, Copilot in Excel and the Researcher agent — became manageable in the Microsoft 365 admin center (2026-07-15); Microsoft-published connectors are enabled by default, partner connectors need admin approval with a 7-day review window; the gallery lists 12 categories and 50+ sources. Microsoft publishes no numeric result/tool/timeout limit for federated connectors. (d) Dynamic tool discovery for MCP plugins (2026-07-16). (d2) The Microsoft 365 Copilot extensibility overview (updated 2026-08-05) now lists FOUR extensibility paths — agents, Copilot connectors (synced into Microsoft Graph, or federated with real-time retrieval over MCP), the Microsoft Work IQ API (which exposes Microsoft 365 data to external agents over both Agent-to-Agent and Model Context Protocol), and the Microsoft 365 Copilot APIs (Retrieval, Search, Chat, Interaction Export, Meeting Insights). Microsoft publishes no numeric tool, token or payload limit for the Work IQ MCP path. (e) SharePoint list knowledge source capped at 20,000 items (2026-07-29). (f) Agent submission to the Agent Store from Agent Builder (2026-07-15), admin-reviewed. (g) Multi-vendor model choice: Anthropic Claude selectable in Copilot Chat from 2026-06-16, Claude Opus 5 from 2026-07-24, Anthropic models in Word from 2026-08-11. Governance unchanged: tenant admins control plugin/agent availability per user and group; distribution via the Microsoft 365 app catalog or AppSource; one declarative agent definition per app package. Adjacent Microsoft surfaces now have their own entries in this file: Copilot Cowork (`microsoft-copilot-cowork`) and Copilot Studio (`microsoft-copilot-studio`).

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf enforcement) is documented for Microsoft 365 Copilot plugins. Plugin manifest 2.4 constrains parameter names by regex and requires `required` values to match declared `properties`, but publishes no property-count or nesting-depth ceiling.

skills_supported.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Declarative agents remain the Microsoft 365 Copilot skills analog: instructions + plugins (tools) + knowledge sources, authored in Agent Builder, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, or Copilot Studio.

skills_loading_model.notes: Agent instructions are always injected. Plugins: all injected when there are 5 or fewer; above 5, semantic matching selects per turn. MCP plugins may additionally resolve their tool list at runtime (dynamic tool discovery), which is partial progressive disclosure. Recorded as always_on because the default small-agent case injects everything.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: Declarative agent instructions (up to 8,000 characters) are injected as system-prompt context every turn. Plugin/tool definitions are injected into the 4,096-token plugin budget that also has to hold tool arguments and tool results — Microsoft's own guidance is to plan for ~66% of it (~2,730 tokens). All functions of a matched plugin are injected even when only one function matched, and Microsoft documents quality degradation above 10 functions/tools per plugin. Dynamic tool discovery (2026-07-16) resolves MCP tool lists at runtime rather than pinning them at publish time, but Microsoft publishes no token saving for it.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Agent instructions plus Microsoft 365 Copilot's own grounding scaffolding are injected per turn. Microsoft publishes no token count for the base system prompt overhead; the only published number in this area remains the 4,096-token plugin scope.

prompt_caching.notes: Changed false→null: Microsoft neither documents nor denies prompt caching at the Microsoft 365 Copilot product layer, and the product is seat-licensed so no cache discount is surfaced to customers. Recording the absence of documentation rather than asserting the feature is off. (Contrast: GitHub Copilot now publishes explicit cached-input rates.)

memory_feature.notes: Microsoft Graph grounding (mail, calendar, files, meetings) plus Work IQ supply per-turn enterprise context that consumes the window. Re-sourced to the Microsoft 365 Copilot release notes, which track the connector/grounding surface continuously; Microsoft publishes no token accounting for it.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No per-token input price exists for Microsoft 365 Copilot: it is sold as a per-user-per-month add-on licence. Token-metered billing in the Microsoft Copilot family appears only in Copilot Studio and Copilot Cowork (Copilot Credits) and in GitHub Copilot (AI Credits) — see those entries.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: No per-token output price is published or charged for the seat-licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot product.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No cached-input rate is published for the seat-licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot product.

batch_discount.notes: No batch-processing discount concept is published for the seat-licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot product.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: No per-token billing exists on the seat-licensed surface, so reasoning tokens are not separately priced or reported to customers.

models.notes: PRODUCT-LAYER ENTRY, refreshed 2026-08-19. Microsoft 365 Copilot is a product layer over a user/tenant-SELECTABLE frontier model — no longer OpenAI-only: Anthropic Claude arrived in Copilot Chat 2026-06-16, Claude Opus 5 on 2026-07-24, and Anthropic models in Word on 2026-08-11. All the numbers here are product-level, not raw model-API limits. Binding MCP limits: 1-10 actions (plugins / MCP servers) per declarative agent (schema 1.8, GA); 5-or-fewer plugins are always injected and above that semantic matching selects per turn; no numeric cap on functions/tools per plugin is published but quality is documented to degrade above 10; the plugin scope has a 4,096-token budget covering context AND response (optimize to ~2,730) and a 45-second timeout; plugin responses cap at 25 items and grounding at 50; tool/grounding calls are sequential, not parallel. New in this window: dynamic tool discovery for MCP plugins (runtime `tools/list` instead of a pinned manifest list), MCP agents inside Word/Excel/PowerPoint/Outlook, MCP-based federated Copilot connectors, and manifest 1.8's EmailActions/MeetingActions. The model-facing `description_for_model` field is now recorded as a 2,048-character soft cap. Cost remains per seat; the price of the Business add-on dropped to a promotional $18/user/month.

release_date.notes: CHANGED from 2023-09-21. The cited page states: 'On November 15, 2023, Microsoft announced that Bing Chat itself was being rebranded under the Copilot name' (the service having launched as Bing Chat on 2023-02-07). knowledge_cutoff.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: Microsoft publishes no knowledge cutoff for consumer Copilot. Smart mode uses 'GPT-5's real-time router to choose the best response approach', so the cutoff would vary per turn with the routed model; web grounding makes recency a retrieval property.

context_window_tokens.notes: CHANGED 200000 → null. The only source for the old figure is a Microsoft Q&A thread answered by an 'Independent Advisor' (not Microsoft) on 2025-07-10, quoting Azure AI Foundry reasoning-model docs for o1/o3-mini — models that no longer back this surface, and the same thread contradicts itself elsewhere. Under this dataset's tiered-evidence rule a context window needs Tier-1 vendor documentation; Microsoft publishes none for consumer Copilot, so the value is null. What is documented: Smart mode uses 'GPT-5's real-time router to choose the best response approach' and Think Deeper uses 'advanced reasoning models by OpenAI', with 'usage limits [that] may apply to certain features and differ for free and Microsoft 365 Premium users'.

input_output_shared.notes: Not documented at the product layer for consumer Copilot; model routing means it would vary per turn in any case.

max_input_tokens.notes: CHANGED 200000 → null, same reasoning as context_window_tokens: the only source was a community Q&A citing retired o1/o3-mini specs, which fails the Tier-1 requirement for a hard limit.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: CHANGED 100000 → null. Community-Q&A-only figure quoting retired reasoning models; no Tier-1 Microsoft source for a consumer Copilot output cap.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: CHANGED 100000 → null, same reasoning as max_output_tokens_default.

extended_context.notes: No numeric extended-context mode is published for consumer Copilot.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Consumer Copilot is free or bundled with a Microsoft 365 Premium subscription and is not token-billed, so reasoning-token accounting is not surfaced.

tokenizer_family.notes: CHANGED from 'o200k_base' → null. Tokenizer identity is a hard field under this dataset's rules and requires Tier-1 vendor documentation; Microsoft publishes none for consumer Copilot, and Smart mode explicitly routes across models per turn ('GPT-5's real-time router'), so no single tokenizer can be asserted. Previously this field cited OpenAI's model docs, which describe OpenAI's API models rather than the Microsoft product.

tokenizer_public.notes: Unknown because the routed model is undisclosed. If the turn lands on an OpenAI model the tiktoken encodings are public; Microsoft neither confirms the model nor the encoding.

tokenizer_access.notes: No Microsoft-provided tokenizer or count-tokens endpoint exists for consumer Copilot. tiktoken can be used as a rough proxy if one assumes an OpenAI-family model, but that assumption is not documented per turn.

count_tokens_method.notes: There is no native count-tokens method for consumer Copilot, and real-time model routing means any local estimate may be against the wrong tokenizer.

image_token_rule.notes: Image upload and generation are supported, but Microsoft publishes no image-to-token conversion rule for consumer Copilot.

max_tools_hard.notes: SOURCE UPGRADED tier 2 → tier 1. The VS Code documentation now states the cap directly: 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time', with the error 'Cannot have more than 128 tools per request.' (Field reports show the runtime variant 'Tool limit exceeded (132/128). Click Configure Tools in the chat input to disable 4 tools and retry'.) SCOPE: AGGREGATE — every enabled tool in the request counts, across all connected MCP servers plus built-in and extension tools; there is no per-MCP-server cap. LAYER: client/host (VS Code + Copilot Chat), not the model API. Mitigation: the `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` setting groups tools behind virtual stubs so large catalogs stay under 128.

max_tools_practical.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 by opening the GitHub engineering blog (published 2025-11-19): GitHub 'trimmed the default 40 built-in tools down to 13 core ones', improving SWE-Lancer and SWEbench-Verified 'success rates by 2-5 percentage points' and cutting latency by 'an average of 400 milliseconds'. Remaining built-ins are grouped into four virtual categories (Jupyter Notebook Tools, Web Interaction Tools, VS Code Workspace Tools, Testing Tools) via embedding-guided routing and adaptive clustering. EMPIRICAL, not a spec: this is the vendor's recommended working-set size, not an enforced cap — MCP servers can push the total far higher, up to the 128 hard cap, with quality falling off.

max_tool_name_len.notes: Still not published by GitHub or the VS Code docs for the Copilot MCP surface. The selected model's own naming constraints apply downstream (e.g. OpenAI-family 64-character function names), and VS Code namespaces MCP tool names, which consumes part of any such budget — but no Copilot-layer number is documented.

max_tool_description_len.notes: Not published for the Copilot MCP surface. The binding pressure is token consumption in the context window, which GitHub addresses qualitatively: 'Disabling unused toolsets also frees up tokens in the AI's context window.'

max_request_size.notes: No request payload size cap is published for the Copilot surface. The binding constraints are the selected model's context window (up to 1M tokens in VS Code and Copilot CLI on supported models) and the 128-tool aggregate cap. Note the billing consequence: input tokens — including every injected tool definition — are metered per model, and crossing the long-context threshold (e.g. > 272K input tokens on GPT-5.5) moves the request into a higher-priced tier.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No separate tool-result size cap is published for GitHub Copilot. Results return as input tokens against the selected model's window and are billed as such.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No per-turn tool-call cycle cap is published for GitHub Copilot. The model context window and the AI-credit budget bound long agent runs indirectly.

max_connected_servers.notes: A limit on the NUMBER of connected MCP servers is not documented in the VS Code or GitHub docs. The binding constraint is aggregate: total enabled tools across every server plus built-ins must stay at or below 128 per request, with `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` grouping surplus tools behind virtual stubs. Practically, a handful of chatty servers reaches 128 quickly — six 30-tool servers already exceed it.

Tool sets are a complementary manual grouping referenced with `#`.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: CLIENT-LAYER LIMITS (GitHub Copilot / VS Code), re-verified 2026-08-19 against Tier-1 VS Code docs. (1) Hard aggregate tool cap: 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time' — across all connected MCP servers plus built-in and extension tools. Errors: 'Cannot have more than 128 tools per request.' / 'Tool limit exceeded (132/128).' (2) Default built-in toolset trimmed from 40 to 13 core tools (2025-11-19), the rest grouped into four virtual categories. (3) `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` groups surplus tools behind virtual stubs so a large catalog stays under 128. (4) Tool sets let a user reference a curated group with `#name`. (5) Tool definitions consume input tokens against the selected model's window and are billed as input under AI Credits. (6) No Copilot-layer tool-name or tool-description length cap is published; the selected model's constraints apply downstream. (7) Extended capability: a 1M-token context window on supported models, available in VS Code and Copilot CLI only, which raises the practical tool budget but increases AI-credit consumption.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: MCP tool definitions are injected as input tokens on every agent-mode turn and are billed as input under AI Credits, so tool-definition bloat has a direct, per-interaction dollar cost as well as a context cost. GitHub states plainly that 'Disabling unused toolsets also frees up tokens in the AI's context window.' The 40→13 default-toolset trim improved benchmark success rates by 2-5 points and cut ~400 ms of latency, which is the clearest vendor evidence that fewer tool definitions is better on both axes. Virtual tools reduce the injected surface by clustering; a 1M-token window (VS Code / Copilot CLI, supported models) raises the ceiling but pushes the request toward higher-priced long-context tiers.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Copilot injects IDE context (open files, selection, recent edits), repository context and the enabled tool definitions each turn. audio_token_rule.notes: Audio is not a listed modality: the model card gives 'Inputs Text, Image' and 'Outputs Text'.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Generic ~4 chars/token rule of thumb, applied for want of a published tokenizer. Treat with extra caution here: Microsoft claims MAI-Code-1.1-Flash needs '25% fewer tokens to complete a task' than version 1.0, implying tokenizer or behaviour changes that a generic ratio will not capture.

function_calling.notes: The model card describes the model as built for 'agentic tool use' and 'tool-using developer scenarios', and it ships as an agent-mode model in GitHub Copilot, where tool calling is the operating mode.

native_mcp.notes: MCP support here is a property of the HOST, not the model: MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is 'Available in GitHub Copilot for all clients' per the model card, and GitHub Copilot speaks MCP natively across IDEs, Copilot CLI, the Copilot app and cloud agents. Microsoft publishes no standalone MCP-capable API endpoint for this model, so its MCP behaviour is whatever the Copilot host provides. Confidence medium for that indirection.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Not documented on the model card or in GitHub's Copilot documentation.

max_tools_hard.notes: No model-layer cap on the number of tools per request is published for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash. The limit that binds in practice is imposed by the host: VS Code enforces 128 enabled tools per chat request (see max_total_tools). Beyond that, the 256K context window is the ceiling — at a typical ~500-800 tokens per MCP tool definition that is a few hundred tool definitions before the window is consumed by tools alone, which is why the host cap bites first.

max_tools_practical.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19: the previous citation (docs.github.com models-and-pricing) was re-opened and contains no tool count at all. The 13 comes from GitHub's engineering blog (2025-11-19, tier 4), re-opened 2026-08-19, which states 'we're rolling out a reduced toolset that trims the default 40 built-in tools down to 13 core ones' and 'we identified a core toolset of 13 essential tools'. NOTE WHAT THAT NUMBER IS: a product decision about the size of the DEFAULT BUILT-IN toolset in VS Code, not a measured degradation threshold, and not measured on MAI-Code-1.1-Flash -- the same post notes 'GitHub Copilot Chat can access hundreds of tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).' EMPIRICAL and inherited from the host surface; no published benchmark isolates this model's tool-selection degradation curve. Confidence low for both reasons; the hard host-layer cap that actually binds is the 128 tools/request in max_total_tools.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No tool-name length constraint is published for this model.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No tool-description length constraint is published for this model.

max_request_size.notes: No request payload size cap is published. The binding constraint is the 256K-token context length; GitHub's Copilot pricing for this model carries no long-context tier, unlike GPT-5.5's '> 272K' tier.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No tool-result size cap is published; results consume the 256K context window as input tokens and are billed at the input rate.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No per-turn tool-call cycle cap is published for this model; the host's agent loop and the AI-credit budget bound long runs instead.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model-layer property. In the VS Code host a limit on the number of connected MCP servers is not documented; the aggregate 128-tool-per-request cap is what binds.

max_total_tools.unit: tools per request (host-layer cap in VS Code, aggregate across all servers)
max_total_tools.notes: HOST-LAYER limit inherited from the surface this model runs on: 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time' (VS Code documentation). Scope: AGGREGATE across all connected MCP servers plus built-in and extension tools. This is not a MAI-Code-1.1-Flash constraint — Microsoft publishes none — but it is the number that actually gates an MCP catalog when this model is selected in Copilot.

tool_definition_shape.value: raw_mcp (as presented by the GitHub Copilot host)
tool_definition_shape.notes: The Copilot host speaks MCP and re-serializes tool definitions into the selected model's native tool format before the request; Microsoft does not publish MAI-Code-1.1-Flash's native tool-definition schema.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Tool definitions are injected into the prompt and billed as input tokens on this surface — GitHub prices MAI-Code-1.1-Flash at $0.20 per 1M input tokens and $0.02 per 1M cached-input tokens, and states that disabling unused toolsets 'frees up tokens in the AI's context window'.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Available through the host, not the model: VS Code's `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` setting groups surplus tools behind virtual stubs so a large catalog stays under the 128-tool cap. Nothing model-specific is published.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: MODEL-LAYER: Microsoft publishes no tool-count, tool-name, tool-description, schema-depth or request-size limits for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash. The model card documents only the 256K context length, a December 2025 pretraining cutoff, text+image input / text output, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts transformer architecture, and support for agentic tool use. HOST-LAYER (GitHub Copilot / VS Code, which is where this model is reachable): 128 enabled tools per chat request, aggregate across all MCP servers and built-in tools; `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` for virtual-tool clustering; tool sets for manual curation. When both layers apply, the host cap binds first.
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Distribution: 'Available in GitHub Copilot for all clients' per the model card, with use inside GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code called out and Copilot CLI support noted as planned for later rollout; GitHub's own reference lists it among supported models but NOT among those offering the 1M-token extended context or configurable reasoning levels. Vendor performance claims versus MAI-Code-1.0: 25% greater token efficiency, tokens stream 25% faster, 25% fewer tokens to complete a task, 22% improvement on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 15% improvement on .NET tasks, code survival up 4%, return visits up 9%, at roughly a quarter of the cost. These are vendor benchmarks, not independent measurements. Closed weights; no Hugging Face card, no self-hosting path.

strict_function_schema.notes: No strict function-schema mode is documented for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash. Recorded as false for absence of any published enforcement, not as a positive statement that arbitrary schemas are accepted.

skills_supported.notes: Via the host rather than the model: when MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is selected in GitHub Copilot, MCP servers supply the tool/skill catalog exactly as they do for any other model in the picker. Microsoft publishes no model-native skills primitive.

skills_loading_model.notes: Inherited from the GitHub Copilot host: enabled tools are presented per request, subject to the 128-tool cap, with virtual tools deferring surplus tools behind stubs.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: MCP tool definitions consume the model's 256K context window as input tokens and are billed at $0.20 per 1M ($0.02 cached). This is the cheapest per-token model in GitHub's Copilot rate table, so an oversized MCP catalog costs less here than on GPT-5.5 ($5.00 input) or Claude Opus 4.5 ($5.00 input) — but it also has the smallest window among the flagship options, since it is excluded from the 1M-token extended-context list. Tool-definition bloat therefore bites on capacity before it bites on cost.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Not published. Overhead is whatever the GitHub Copilot host injects (IDE context, repository context, enabled tool definitions); Microsoft publishes no model-side system-prompt token accounting.

prompt_caching.notes: GitHub's Copilot rate table lists a cached-input price of $0.02 per 1M tokens for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash against $0.20 uncached — a 90% discount — which confirms prompt caching is active for this model on the Copilot surface. No cache-write cost is listed (that applies only to GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna). Microsoft publishes no cache TTL, minimum cacheable prefix or breakpoint control.

memory_feature.notes: No model-native persistent memory is documented; session context is supplied by the host.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: GitHub Copilot models-and-pricing table, verified 2026-08-19: MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is listed as GA in the Lightweight category at $0.20 per 1M input tokens. Billed as AI Credits at 1 credit = $0.01 USD. Microsoft publishes no independent API price for this model outside the Copilot surface.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: GitHub Copilot models-and-pricing table, verified 2026-08-19: $1.20 per 1M output tokens — a 6x input-to-output ratio, and the cheapest output rate in GitHub's table (compare GPT-5.5 at $30.00 and Claude Opus 4.5 at $25.00).

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: GitHub Copilot models-and-pricing table, verified 2026-08-19: $0.02 per 1M cached-input tokens, a 90% discount on the $0.20 uncached input rate. No cache-write cost applies to this model.

batch_discount.notes: No batch-processing discount is published; the exposed cost levers on the Copilot surface are cached input and model choice.

billing_unit.notes: Billed through GitHub Copilot's AI Credits system (1 AI credit = $0.01 USD) at the per-model token rates above. There is no separate Microsoft-hosted pay-per-token endpoint for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash documented at Tier 1 as of 2026-08-19.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Image input is a listed modality on the model card, but GitHub's rate table publishes only text-token rates for this model and no separate image-token price.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Not documented. This model is not on GitHub's configurable-reasoning-levels list, and the rate table has no reasoning-token column.

models.notes: NEW ENTRY (added 2026-08-19). MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is Microsoft's own first-party agentic coding model, released 2026-08-11 and in production in GitHub Copilot. It is included here because it is a Microsoft model shipped inside a Microsoft Copilot surface, and because it is the ONLY entity in this vendor's file with a Tier-1 published context window: 'Context length 256K tokens' per the official Microsoft AI model card. Also published: December 2025 pretraining cutoff, text+image input / text output, sparse Mixture-of-Experts transformer, agentic tool use. It supersedes MAI-Code-1-Flash (2026-06-02) — that predecessor has no entry in this file and is not added, since only the current-generation model belongs in the roster. MCP and tool limits are HOST-supplied, not model-supplied: reachable only through GitHub Copilot, where VS Code's aggregate 128-tools-per-request cap binds. No tokenizer is published, so token counts on this model cannot be reproduced locally — a real gap given Microsoft's claim of '25% fewer tokens to complete a task'. Pricing is Tier-1 and concrete: $0.20 input / $0.02 cached input / $1.20 output per 1M tokens, the cheapest in GitHub's Copilot rate table.
